standard.title: Who They Are and Their World
standard.description: investigate who they are and the people in their world
standard.prior_knowledge: No prior HPE curriculum. Students bring lived experience of family, community and personal identity. No prior structured curriculum investigation of identity and belonging.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate who they are and the people in their world, making connections between identity, belonging and community.

nodes.label: Personal identity and belonging
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can make personal connections between their identity and their sense of belonging — who they are, where they come from, the people in their lives.
nodes.minimum_width: Share something about who they are — including at least one aspect of family, culture or personal interest — and connect this to a story or text about identity and belonging.
nodes.typical_width: Explore personal identity through stories, discussion and creative expression; make connections between personal qualities, family background and belonging in class and community contexts.
wider: Explore identity and belonging stories from First Nations Australian contexts, discussing similarities and differences with their own experience
Investigate cultural practices from different cultures, including cultures of Asia, that are important to families and communities
Explore how belonging to groups (family, class, community) shapes identity and personal connections
nodes.hinge_reason: A secure sense of personal identity is the conceptual foundation for investigating others and differences (next node). Students who cannot articulate aspects of their own identity cannot meaningfully compare or connect with others' identities and family structures.

response_modes.reason: Identity is expressed through multiple lenses — family, culture, physical strengths, community. Varied expression modes (drawing, story, movement, talk) allow all students to access this concept from their own starting point.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-cultural and First Nations identity stories provide pedagogically rich material for genuine investigation of diverse belonging experiences — not just self-description.
success_criteria: Shares at least one aspect of who they are or where they come from
Makes a connection between something about themselves and a feeling of belonging to a group or community

nodes.label: Families and communities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify different family structures and explore similarities and differences across communities and cultures.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify their own family structure and at least one other type of family structure that is different from their own.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss a range of family structures; explore similarities and differences in families across First Nations Australian communities and other cultures; recognise the right to belong and contribute.
wider: Compare family structures and community roles across First Nations Australian communities with students' own experience
Investigate how families from different cultural backgrounds, including cultures of Asia, organise themselves and their practices
Explore community contributions — how each person, including themselves, contributes to a group

response_modes.reason: Family diversity is the content here — restrict to generalising across types. Use texts, images and discussion rather than requiring personal disclosure from students about their own family.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations and cross-cultural family structures provide genuine breadth beyond the nuclear-family default, and ACARA elaborations explicitly foreground this direction.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two different types of family structures
Describes one similarity or difference between families in different communities or cultures

nodes.label: Strengths and contribution
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify personal strengths and recognise how they contribute to group success and a sense of belonging.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one personal strength and describe one way they have helped themselves or others in a physical or group activity.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss personal strengths in physical and social contexts; connect strengths to contributions in group situations; recognise that everyone has a right to belong and contribute.
wider: Explore how different strengths contribute to team success in varied physical activity contexts
Connect the idea of contribution to belonging — what it feels like to be valued in a group
Investigate how First Nations Australian communities recognise and value different strengths and roles

response_modes.reason: This node integrates personal identity (N1) and community belonging (N2) — strengths connect who you are with how you contribute. Design activities that surface both simultaneously.

success_criteria: Names at least one personal strength
Describes one way their strength has helped them or others in a shared activity
